portal.title: Accounting & Finance Portal
portal.subtitle: From Foundation to Professionalism
portal.desc: An integrated educational platform aimed at simplifying complex accounting concepts and presenting them in a practical format that fits current market needs.
portal.accounting_definition: Accounting is not just recording numbers, but an integrated system for collecting, analyzing, and classifying financial data, and transforming it into valuable information that supports strategic decision-making in organizations.
portal.performance_desc: Helps in knowing how efficiently the company uses its available resources.
portal.compliance_desc: Ensures commitment to professional standards and prevailing tax laws.
portal.core_pillars_desc: Understanding these elements is the first step for any successful accountant seeking professional excellence.
portal.assets_desc: Everything owned by the entity that has future economic value.
portal.assets_example: Example: Cash, machinery, and real estate.
portal.liabilities_desc: Obligations and debts owed by the entity to external parties.
portal.equity_desc: Represents the owners' share in the net value of the entity after deducting obligations.
portal.revenue_desc: Increase in assets as a result of selling goods or providing services to customers.
portal.revenue_example: Example: Sales of goods and services.
portal.expenses_desc: Costs incurred by the entity in order to achieve revenue.
portal.full_cycle_desc: Track financial transaction steps from the moment they occur as initial analysis, up to journal entries and reaching their culmination in the final financial statements.

accounting_cycle.title: Accounting Cycle
accounting_cycle.subtitle: The accounting cycle is a set of organized steps through which financial transactions are recorded and analyzed, leading to the preparation of financial statements. This cycle helps ensure data accuracy and sound financial decision-making.
accounting_cycle.learn_more_prompt: Want to learn more or apply this to your company?
accounting_cycle.learn_more_desc: We are here to help you build a strong and accurate accounting system following global best practices.

steps.analysis_desc: The accounting process begins with analyzing financial transactions to determine their nature and impact on various accounts such as assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses, ensuring they are recorded correctly.
steps.analysis_example: Determining if the operation represents an asset purchase, liability settlement, or revenue realization.
steps.journal_desc: Journal entries are the basic step in recording financial operations, where each operation is proven in the form of an accounting entry based on the debit and credit system to ensure balance and accuracy.
steps.journal_example: Recording an entry from Purchase A/C to Cash A/C when purchasing for cash.
steps.ledger_desc: In the general ledger, all journal entries are collected and posted to independent accounts, which helps in knowing the balance of each account clearly and organized.
steps.ledger_example: Posting all cash movements to the Cash account page in the general ledger.
steps.trial_balance_desc: The trial balance is used to ensure the balance of accounts, where the total of debit balances must equal the total of credit balances, reflecting the accuracy of accounting recording.
steps.trial_balance_example: Ensuring that the total debit balances equals the total credit balances before preparing financial statements.
steps.adjustments_desc: Adjusting entries aim to modify accounts at the end of the financial period to ensure that revenues and expenses are recorded in the correct period, such as accrued expenses and depreciation.
steps.adjustments_example: Calculating and proving annual depreciation expense for fixed assets.

tax.tax_desc: It is a specialized branch of accounting that focuses on calculating taxes due on the entity according to the tax laws and legislation applicable in Egypt. It aims to determine the tax base accurately and submit returns on their legal dates.
tax.types_subtitle: A quick look at the tax obligations facing Egyptian companies.
tax.corporate_tax_desc: Imposed on the net profits of legal persons (companies).
tax.vat_desc: An indirect tax imposed on most goods and services.
tax.salary_tax_desc: Deducted from employees' salaries and supplied to the Tax Authority.
tax.withholding_tax_desc: Amounts deducted under the tax account when dealing with suppliers.
tax.corporate_detail_subtitle: Income tax is considered the basic tax on corporate profits in Egypt.
tax.subject_desc: All companies and institutions (legal persons) resident in Egypt are subject for all their profits, whether achieved in Egypt or abroad, and non-resident companies for their profits achieved in Egypt only.
tax.base_desc: It is the net accounting profit after making the necessary tax adjustments (additions and deductions) to reach the actually taxable profit.
tax.provisions: Provisions and reserves of all kinds.
tax.fines_penalties: Fines and financial penalties resulting from violations.
tax.ngo_donations: Donations to recognized associations (within the limits of 10/110).

construction.def_desc: It is a specialized branch of financial accounting that aims to track costs and revenues for each construction project separately, due to the nature of the activity that depends on the "Job Order System" or "Projects".
construction.diff_title: Difference between Commercial and Construction Accounting:
construction.diff_desc: In commercial accounting, ready-made goods are sold in a fast cash cycle, while in construction, the product (building) is "manufactured" at the customer's site and for long periods of time that may exceed the financial year.
construction.importance_desc: Its importance lies in strict control over costs (materials, labor, subcontractors) to ensure that the estimated budget is not exceeded and the target profit is achieved.

construction.cycle_step5_desc: Recording accrual, collection, and retention entries.
construction.cycle_step6_desc: Comparing actual cost with estimated cost and determining the final profit.
construction.poc_desc: It is the approved method for recognizing revenue in long-term contracts, where part of the revenue and profit is recognized based on what has actually been spent compared to the total estimated cost.
construction.formula_desc: Completion Rate = (Actual cost-to-date ÷ Total estimated cost) × 100

construction.why_poc_title: Why do we use this method?
construction.matching_principle: Achieving the Matching Principle of matching revenues with expenses.
construction.fair_pos: Showing the fair financial position of the company during the execution years.
construction.avoid_fluctuation: Avoid large profit fluctuations when projects end only.
construction.extracts_desc: An extract is the official document by which the contractor demands the client to pay amounts in exchange for the works that have already been implemented in the site during a specific period.
construction.extract_initial_desc: Issued at the beginning of the project to pay the advance payment.
construction.extract_current_desc: Issued periodically (mostly monthly) to follow up on work progress.
construction.extract_final_desc: Issued at project completion and initial handover.
construction.calc_net_extract: How to calculate net extract value
construction.taxes_subtitle: Legal and sovereign obligations for construction and building activity.
construction.vat_desc: Construction is subject to Schedule Tax (5%) or the General Rate (14%) depending on the nature of the contract (supply and installation or operation only).

construction.eng_stamps_desc: Fees imposed on contracts and extracts for the benefit of the Engineers Syndicate.
construction.residential_desc: Focuses on excavation, reinforced concrete, and building stages, with massive material costs.
construction.finishing_desc: Depends heavily on subcontractors (electricity, plumbing, carpentry) and high labor costs.
construction.road_desc: Depends on the cost of heavy equipment (rollers, asphalt mixers) and fuel consumption.

reconciliation_page.title: Bank Reconciliation Statement
reconciliation_page.subtitle: Learn how to match bank book balance with actual bank statement.

intro.definition_desc: An analytical report matching the bank balance in company records with the balance in the actual bank statement.
intro.goal_desc: To ensure cash balance accuracy and detect errors or unrecorded transactions.

components.title: Reasons for Differences
items: Deposits in Transit: Money sent to bank but not yet in statement.
Outstanding Checks: Checks issued by company but not yet cashed.
Bank Charges: Fees deducted by bank not yet in company books.
NSF Checks: Checks deposited by company but rejected by bank.
Errors: Recording errors by bank or company.

steps.title: Preparation Steps
items: Add Deposits in Transit, subtract Outstanding Checks.
Add Interest income, subtract Bank Charges and NSF Checks.
Final Adjusted Balance must match on both sides.

example.title: Practical Example
example.desc: Bank statement balance $52,000, Outstanding checks $5,000, Deposits in transit $2,000.

entries.title: Required Adjustment Entries
entries.desc: Transactions not yet in books must be recorded after reconciliation.
entries.entry1: Bank Charges: Dr. Bank Charges .. Cr. Bank
entries.entry2: Interest: Dr. Bank .. Cr. Interest Income

intro.title: Inventory Overview
intro.definition_desc: Inventory refers to the goods and products held by a business for resale or use in production. It is a key current asset, and its valuation directly affects Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and net profit.
intro.definition: Inventory refers to the goods and products held by a business for resale or use in production. It is a key current asset.
intro.desc: Effective inventory management ensures the right balance between demand and storage costs.
intro.importance_desc: Helps in reducing costs, preventing spoilage, ensuring product availability, and improving cash flow.

items: Improving business cash flow and liquidity

methods.title: Valuation Methods
methods.subtitle: Accounting methods vary based on the flow of goods and financial policy.

fifo.title: First-In, First-Out (FIFO)
fifo.desc: Assumes that the goods purchased first are the ones sold first. Ending inventory is valued at most recent prices.
fifo.example: Example: Bought 100 units at $10, then 200 at $12. If 150 sold, cost is 100*$10 + 50*$12.
fifo.impact_desc: Impact: Results in higher profits during inflation and inventory value close to market price.
fifo.impact: Impact: Results in higher profits during inflation and inventory value close to market price.

lifo.title: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO)
lifo.desc: Assumes that the most recently purchased goods are sold first. (Note: Not allowed under IFRS).
lifo.example: Example: (same data) If 150 units sold, cost is 150 units at $12 (latest purchase).
lifo.impact_desc: Impact: Often used to reduce taxes during price hikes as it increases COGS.
lifo.impact: Impact: Often used to reduce taxes during price hikes as it increases COGS.

average.title: Weighted Average
average.desc: Average cost per unit is calculated by dividing total cost of goods available by total units.
average.formula: Average Cost = Total Cost / Total Quantity
average.impact_desc: Impact: Provides middle-ground results and smooths out price fluctuations.
average.impact: Impact: Provides middle-ground results and smooths out price fluctuations.

accrual.title: Accrual Principle
accrual.desc: Recording financial transactions when they occur regardless of the timing of cash receipt or payment.
accrual.example: Recording the electricity bill for December as an "accrued expense" even if it is not paid until January.

going_concern.title: Going Concern Principle
going_concern.desc: The assumption that the entity is continuing its activity for a long period of time and is not subject to liquidation soon.
going_concern.example: Valuing fixed assets at historical cost instead of their current liquidation value.

consistency.title: Consistency Principle
consistency.desc: Using the same accounting methods and policies from one period to another to ensure comparability.
consistency.example: If the company chooses the "Straight Line" method for depreciation, it must adhere to it in upcoming years.

materiality.title: Materiality Principle
materiality.desc: Focusing on information whose omission or misstatement affects the decisions of financial statement users.
materiality.example: Considering the purchase of a "calculator" an immediate expense instead of a fixed asset due to its small value relative to the company size.

full_disclosure.title: Full Disclosure Principle
full_disclosure.desc: Providing all necessary information that matters to financial statement users to make their decisions.
full_disclosure.example: Adding disclosures about existing legal cases against the company in the attached notes.

prudence.title: Prudence (Conservatism) Principle
prudence.desc: Not overestimating assets and revenues, and immediate recognition of expected losses.
prudence.example: Creating an "allowance for doubtful accounts" when a customer is expected not to pay their debts.

comparability.title: Comparability Principle
comparability.desc: Enabling users to compare the entity's financial statements over time or with other entities.
comparability.example: Displaying current year figures alongside previous year figures in the financial statements.

ias1.title: Presentation of Financial Statements
ias1.desc: Sets requirements for the presentation of financial statements to ensure comparability.
ias1.usage: Used as a primary guide for structuring the balance sheet and income statement.

ias2.title: Inventories
ias2.desc: Determines the accounting treatment for inventory and measurement of its cost.
ias2.usage: Applied to value goods in warehouses at the end of the financial year.

ias7.title: Statement of Cash Flows

ias16.title: Property, Plant and Equipment

ias16.usage: Applied to calculate depreciation and recognize productive assets.

ifrs16.title: Leases
ifrs16.desc: Requires lessees to recognize assets and liabilities for all leases.
ifrs16.usage: Used to show long-term lease obligations within the balance sheet.

ifrs9.title: Financial Instruments
ifrs9.desc: Addresses the classification and measurement of financial assets and liabilities.
ifrs9.usage: Applied to evaluate investments, stocks, and bonds owned by the company.

eas16.desc: Addresses the accounting treatment for fixed assets and depreciation calculation.

depreciation_page.title: Accounting Depreciation Methods
depreciation_page.subtitle: A comprehensive guide on distributing fixed asset costs over their useful life.
depreciation_page.featured_desc: Deepen your knowledge with our specialized modules on complex accounting treatments.

intro.definition_desc: The process of distributing fixed asset costs (machines, cars, buildings) over their estimated useful life to reflect consumption and value decrease over time.
intro.goal_desc: Aims to apply the matching principle (matching revenue with expense) and determine fair value for assets on the balance sheet.

sl.title: Straight-Line Method
sl.desc: Simplest and most common; cost is distributed equally over the useful life years.
sl.example: Asset cost $100k, salvage $10k, life 5 yrs. Depreciation = $18,000 per year.
sl.entry: Entry: Dr. Depreciation Expense .. Cr. Accumulated Depreciation

db.title: Declining Balance Method
db.desc: Higher expense in early years; suitable for fast-obsoleting tech assets.
db.formula: Depreciation = Beginning Book Value × Depreciation Rate
db.entry: Entry: Dr. Depreciation Expense .. Cr. Accumulated Depreciation

uop.title: Units of Production
uop.desc: Links depreciation to actual activity (hours or units produced) rather than time.
uop.formula: Depreciation Rate per Unit = (Cost - Salvage) / Total Estimated Units
uop.example: Machine produces 100k units. If 20k produced in Yr 1, dep is 20% of cost.
uop.entry: Entry: Dr. Depreciation Expense .. Cr. Accumulated Depreciation

rows.impact: High initial impact, decreases over time

tax_impact.title: Tax Impact of Depreciation
tax_impact.desc: Depreciation is a tax-deductible expense, which reduces taxable net profit and thus provides cash liquidity to the entity.

intro.definition_desc: Scrap refers to material residue from the manufacturing process that cannot be used in the original product, or fixed assets that reached the end of their useful life.

production.title: Production Scrap
production.desc: Like wood residue, fabric scraps, or metal shavings in factories.

assets.title: Asset Scrap
assets.desc: Assets fully depreciated or disposed of and sold as wreckage.

sale.title: Sale Case
sale.desc: Selling value is considered incidental income or a reduction in production cost depending on materiality.
sale.entry: Entry: Dr. Cash .. Cr. Miscellaneous Income (Scrap)

reuse.title: Internal Reuse
reuse.desc: When scrap is used in another production process to reduce new material costs.
reuse.entry: Entry: Dr. Material Control (A) .. Cr. Material Control (B)

control.title: Scrap Control
items: Allocating a specific and secure area for scrap storage.
Issuing an inventory addition note for each scrap quantity.
Selling through a specialized committee at best market price.

example.entry: Entry: 5,000 Dr. Cash .. 5,000 Cr. Scrap Sale Income

cost.title: Cost Accounting
cost.hero_title: Achieve Maximum Efficiency and Profit Control
cost.hero_subtitle: Specialized cost accounting systems help you calculate product costs accurately and identify waste points to improve competitiveness.
cost.cost_accounting_desc: Cost accounting is an internal accounting system that tracks and analyzes all costs incurred by the company to produce a product or provide a service. It provides management with the data needed to make decisions about pricing, productivity, and control.
cost.diff_financial_desc: Cost accounting focuses on internal details and specific products, while financial accounting focuses on the overall entity for external parties.
cost.pricing_desc: Determining the minimum selling price that covers costs and achieves the targeted profit margin.
cost.control_eval_desc: Comparing actual costs with standard costs to detect deviations and address them promptly.
cost.core_elements_subtitle: Every product or service cost is fundamentally composed of three main elements.
cost.direct_materials_desc: Main materials that enter directly into manufacturing the product and can be easily traced.
cost.direct_materials_examples: Wood in furniture, iron in construction, fabric in clothes.
cost.direct_labor_desc: Wages of workers who work directly on producing the product or providing the service.
cost.indirect_costs_desc: Costs necessary for production but not directly linked to a specific unit of product.
cost.indirect_costs_examples: Factory rent, electricity, indirect labor (guards, supervisors).
cost.orders_system_desc: Used for products made according to specific customer requests.
cost.process_system_desc: Used for mass production of similar products in continuous stages.
cost.standard_system_desc: Estimating costs in advance and comparing them with actual results.
cost.abc_system_desc: Allocating indirect costs based on the activities that consume those costs.
cost.tools_subtitle: Simple tools to help you perform basic cost calculations and analyze profitability.
cost.break_even_desc: The volume of sales at which total revenue equals total costs (Zero Profit).
cost.industrial_cost_desc: Summary of all costs incurred to manufacture products during a period.
cost.deviation_desc: Detecting differences between estimated and actual costs for each production element.
cost.margin_desc: Evaluating the profitability of each product and its contribution to covering fixed costs.
cost.cost_centers_desc: Tracing and analyzing expenses for each department or production line independently.
cost.cta_title: Want to implement a professional cost system in your factory or project?
cost.cta_desc: Our team provides specialized consultations to design and implement cost systems that ensure you have a clear vision of every penny spent.

bad_debts_page.title: Bad Debts and Accounting Treatment
bad_debts_page.subtitle: Understanding the difference between doubtful and bad debts and protecting financial statements.
bad_debts_page.risk_mgmt_desc: Ensure your balance sheet reflects true realizable value through strategic allowances.

intro.definition_desc: These are amounts that a business has lost hope of collecting from customers due to bankruptcy or disappearance, considered a realized loss that must be recognized.
intro.diff_desc: Doubtful debts are debts we expect not to collect (possibility), while bad debts are debts we are certain will not be collected (certainty).

direct.title: Direct Write-off Method
direct.desc: The debt is written off directly to an expense account when its loss is confirmed. Suitable for small businesses.
direct.entry: Entry: Dr. Bad Debt Expense .. Cr. Accounts Receivable

allowance.title: Allowance Method (Alternative)
allowance.desc: Following the prudence principle, an allowance is created to meet expected losses before they actually occur.
allowance.entry_forming: Creating Allowance: Dr. Bad Debt Expense .. Cr. Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
allowance.entry_writing_off: Actual Write-off: Dr. Allowance for Doubtful Accounts .. Cr. Accounts Receivable

recovery.title: Recovery of Written-off Debts
recovery.desc: If a customer pays after their debt was written off, the entry is reversed to record the collection.
recovery.entry: Collection Entry: (1) Dr. Accounts Receivable Cr. Bad Debt Recovery | (2) Dr. Cash Cr. Accounts Receivable

example.title: Practical Example
example.desc: A customer owing $10,000 declared bankruptcy. Company decides to write off using Allowance method.
example.allowance_entry: Allowance Entry: Dr. Allowance for Doubtful Accounts | Cr. Accounts Receivable
example.direct_entry: Direct Entry: Dr. Bad Debt Expense | Cr. Accounts Receivable
example.entry: Entry: $10,000 Dr. Allowance for Doubtful Accounts | $10,000 Cr. Accounts Receivable
